On revenue: revenue = flights × seats × load factor × average fare. We're told load factor is roughly unchanged, so the drop is either fewer flights flown or a lower average fare — or a mix shift toward cheaper routes or cheaper fare classes. $176M on $200M is a 12% decline.

On cost: fuel, labor, maintenance, ownership/lease, airport fees, distribution. I'd want to know whether total cost actually held flat at $180M or grew.

To start: do we have the breakdown of revenue into flights flown and average fare per passenger for FY2023 versus FY2025? And the cost base split by line item for both years?
said: A revenue-versus-cost split. Before any data: is that framework MECE — what's missing, and which branch would you prioritize first, and why?

candidateText:
I think revenue and cost together is exhaustive at the top level — operating profit is just the difference, so nothing escapes it. Where it's not clean is inside the buckets. Fuel, for example, shows up as a cost but it's partly volume-driven, so if I cut flights it moves both sides; I'd need to be careful not to double-count when I size drivers.

What it's missing is a couple of things that don't sit neatly in either box. One is the network dimension — six cities, and the average could be hiding one or two routes bleeding money while the rest are fine. Second is the competitive and demand context: did a low-cost carrier enter, did a corporate customer leave, did the hub partner change schedules. And third, the distribution channel — we sell mainly through our own site, so if that mix shifted it affects net fare.

So I'd add a route-level cut underneath revenue.
said: Understood. On what you asked about earlier: Across all six routes, revenue fell from $200.0M to $176.0M and contribution fell from $40.0M to $16.0M, on 14,000 flights a year — the same number of flights in both years. On the revenue breakdown by fares and extras, passenger counts and average fare: we'll get there in a bit. With those figures, what do they tell you about where the revenue decline is coming from, and what would you look at next?
replayNote: Report fault: scoring is not replayed. Wave: report statements about what the candidate said are true to the transcript; the hand grade's report read sees it.

grade.note: Report, Quantitative: "The first attempt at the Lakeport fare math was garbled and left extras out. It was corrected only after the interviewer asked." His $105 was revenue per seat (the error was the load), and he corrected it himself.

candidateText:
Revenue per flight went from $200M/14,000 = $14,286 to $176M/14,000 = $12,571 — down about $1,714 per flight, roughly 12%.

Contribution per flight: $40M/14,000 = $2,857, down to $16M/14,000 = $1,143. So contribution fell $1,714 per flight too — exactly the revenue decline. Variable cost per flight is flat.

So this isn't a cost story at the flight level at all. Flights are constant, loads are constant, so seats sold are constant — the entire $24M is price. Average fare is down about 12%.

That pushes me to ask why fare fell. Two candidates: we're discounting to hold those loads, or the mix shifted toward cheaper fare classes or cheaper routes. Do we have fare and traffic by route for both years?
said: Mm-hm. Here's an exhibit: Larkspur Air — Results by route, FY2023 vs. FY2025 ($ millions unless noted). What does it tell you about where the decline is concentrated?
replayNote: Report fault: scoring is not replayed. Wave: report says who corrected what as the transcript shows; the hand grade's report read sees it.

grade.note: "I don't have contribution by departure time." True (no item holds a time-of-day cut).

candidateText:
A few levers. The gap is $600 per flight, or $10 per passenger.

First, extras. We're at $20 per passenger. Pushing that to $30 — bag fees, paid seat assignment, maybe a loyalty or card partnership — closes the whole gap without touching fare. That's a 50% lift on ancillaries, aggressive but not impossible given we sell direct on our own site.

Second, variable cost. $9,000 per flight: fuel $4,000, crew $2,000, maintenance $1,500, fees $1,500. A 7% cut gets us there. Airport fee renegotiation at Lakeport and Port Avery, crew scheduling productivity, fuel burn practices.

Third, differentiate rather than match. If the low-cost carrier is a no-frills product and we're selling direct with a better schedule, maybe we hold a $10–15 premium on business travelers instead of matching to the dollar.

Fourth, cut frequency to only the flights that clear $9,000 — fly the peaks, drop the thin midday departures.

Do we have a sense of how contribution varies by departure time on those routes?
said: Four levers on the existing routes. I don't have contribution by departure time. An exhibit for you — Proposed new routes — Planning estimates (average per flight across Hub–Ashford and Hub–Brookhaven). What stands out to you in this exhibit?

grade.note: "are the fixed costs truly fixed if we shrink" → aircraft_leases.

candidateText:
It confirms it's a competitive price story, not demand or cost: we held volume by giving up fare, and we matched all the way down below our own variable cost. Both routes now destroy cash on every flight — Lakeport –$1.2M, Port Avery –$0.6M.

But exiting alone isn't enough. If we drop both, contribution goes from $16M to $17.8M against $20M fixed, so we're still at –$2.2M. The gap is $2.2M more.

Two things I want. First, are the fixed costs truly fixed if we shrink — does any of the $20M come off with fewer destinations, or is it hub and overhead? Second, and more important: those 5,000 flights free up aircraft. Can we redeploy them to the four uncontested routes or a new city? At Westhaven-like economics, $1,900 contribution per flight, that's real money.

Also — how did fare fall over FY2024 versus FY2025? If it's still sliding, matching has no floor.
said: You've got the exit math and a redeployment idea. All nine aircraft are leased through 2030, so returning them early is not an option. I'll come back to the fare trend across FY2024 and FY2025 shortly. On redeploying those freed aircraft, you cited Westhaven-like economics per flight. Before we use that, what would you want to confirm about whether new flights would actually earn that?

candidateText:
Okay, this is informative. Flights are flat at 14,000 both years, so capacity didn't change — 14,000 × 80 seats = 1.12 million seats a year, same in both periods. And contribution fell exactly as much as revenue, $24M to $24M, which means variable cost per flight didn't move at all. So the entire problem is on the revenue line, not the cost line.

Let me get at fare. $176.0M over 14,000 flights is $12,571 per flight. Against FY2023's $200.0M over the same 14,000, that's $14,286. So our average fare dropped from about $14,286 to $12,571 — roughly a 12% decline in what we're getting per passenger.

That's a pure pricing story. Do we have the route-level split of that $176M, and whether a competitor entered on any of the six?
said: Understood. Early in FY2024, a low-cost airline started nonstop flights on Hub–Lakeport and Hub–Port Avery, and it hasn't entered Larkspur's other four routes; Larkspur cut its fares to match, and its planes stayed just as full. Here's an exhibit: Larkspur Air — Results by route, FY2023 vs. FY2025 ($ millions unless noted). Before the competitor question, what does the route picture tell you, and does it still support calling this a pure pricing story?

grade.note: Probe on her flagged $18,000 (a unit error).

candidateText:
That's a hard structural gap. Let me put numbers on it.

Our variable cost is $9,000 per flight. Thirty percent lower puts the competitor at $6,300 per flight. At the current $120 fare with 60 passengers, they're taking in $8,400 — the same $8,400 we take — but against $6,300, so they're making $2,100 a flight where we lose $600. They can sit at this fare indefinitely and we can't.

The other way to see it: to break even at $9,000 we need $150 per passenger, so $130 fare plus $20 extras. The market price is $120. We're $10 short on fare and there's no path to raising it while they're there, because they'd just hold.

So matching price was the wrong move — we kept the planes full at 75% and bought nothing for it. Do we know whether load factor would actually fall if we priced back up to $200, or is that untested?
said: Mm-hm. You said “$18,000” — can you show me that calculation step by step?

grade.note: Probe on her $2,800 contribution (75% load for the exhibit's 70%).

candidateText:
Two things. First, no incumbent on either route, so we're not walking into the same price war — the $180 fare should hold rather than get matched down.

Second, the ramp. At 60% in year one that's 48 passengers a flight, times $200 per passenger = $9,600 per flight, against $9,200 variable cost. So $400 of contribution per flight, times 5,000 = $2.0M in year one — versus the $14.0M at steady state. So the first twelve months are thin but still positive, and still better than the negative $1.8M we're bleeding today.

That's a $3.8M swing inside the 12-month window the CEO asked for, which takes us from minus $4M to roughly minus $0.2M. Not quite breakeven in year one, but profitable from year two.

Do we know how quickly we can exit the Lakeport and Port Avery slots?
said: Right. You had "$2,800" of contribution per flight earlier. How did you do that calculation, given the load factor on the exhibit?

candidateText:
This is extremely concentrated. Four routes are basically flat — Cedar Bluff, Granite Falls, Millbrook, Westhaven move by less than half a million each. The entire problem is Lakeport and Port Avery.

Lakeport: revenue 26.4 down to 16.8, so -$9.6M, and contribution swings from +8.4 to -1.2, a $9.6M hit. Port Avery: revenue 46.8 down to 31.0, so -$15.8M, with contribution going from +13.8 to -0.6, a $14.4M swing. Together that's about $25M of revenue decline and $24M of contribution decline — the whole story.

What strikes me is that on both routes contribution fell roughly one-for-one with revenue, meaning they were high-margin routes that got competed away. Lakeport was running 32% contribution margin, Port Avery about 29% — well above the other four at 13–15%. Those were the premium, probably monopoly routes.

Do we know whether a competitor entered Lakeport and Port Avery, and what fares did there?
said: Right. Early in FY2024, a low-cost airline started nonstop flights on Hub–Lakeport and Hub–Port Avery, and it hasn't entered Larkspur's other four routes; Larkspur cut its fares to match, and its planes stayed just as full. The low-cost airline's cost per seat is about 30% lower than Larkspur's — it flies larger planes and has lower labor costs — and its fares are about the same as Larkspur's current fares. You got 1.16M seats from 14,500 flights times 80. What flight count is that resting on?

grade.note: Late probe quoting its claim ("On the $115 fare with 15% fewer passengers …").

candidateText:
Correction first: I said $105 a seat earlier — that was wrong. It's $120 fare plus $20 extras = $140 per passenger, 60 passengers, so $8,400 per flight against $9,000 variable. Minus $600 a flight, times 2,000 = –$1.2M. Matches the exhibit.

Now my fare idea. Break-even needs $9,000 per flight. If I hold 60 passengers I need $150 total per head, so a $130 fare — up 8%. But raise fare against a competitor at the same price with 30% lower cost and I lose far more than 8% of traffic. Say fare to $140, total $160, and I lose 15%: 51 pax × $160 = $8,160. Still worse than today.

So raising fare doesn't work at 75% load. The structural point is their cost per seat is 30% below ours and they can price anywhere we can go. We cannot win Lakeport on price.
said: Understood, you reworked the fare option. On the $115 fare with 15% fewer passengers, what revenue per flight do you get, and how does it compare with today's $8,400?

candidateText:
Cut frequency to protect fare, promote hard into the hub's connecting base, and look at seasonality before concluding it's structural. Up front I'd have wanted market-size and competitor presence data on Ashford and Brookhaven, plus a phased exit so one jet stayed on an old route as a fallback.

I'm done — can we do another case?
said: We've covered everything I wanted to. Thanks for working through the case — your written report will follow.
